text: Amcor plc, originally incorporated as Arctic Jersey Limited under the laws of the Bailiwick of Jersey in July 2018 to facilitate its merger with Bemis Company, Inc., was renamed Amcor plc and became a public limited company under the same jurisdiction on October 10, 2018. On June 11, 2019, Amcor completed the acquisition of Bemis Company, Inc. pursuant to a definitive merger agreement dated August 6, 2018, under which Bemis shareholders received 5.1 Amcor shares for each Bemis share, and Amcor shareholders received one Amcor CHESS Depositary Instrument (CDI) for each Amcor Limited share outstanding. Following the transaction, Amcor shares were registered with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission and traded on the New York Stock Exchange under the symbol "AMCR," while CDIs were traded on the Australian Securities Exchange under the symbol "AMC." Amcor Limited shares were delisted from the ASX, and Bemis shares were delisted from the NYSE. The Company’s business strategy centers on a focused portfolio of strong businesses in flexible and rigid packaging, specialty cartons, and closures, driven by a focus on primary packaging for fast-moving consumer goods, favorable industry structures, attractive relative growth, and multiple competitive advantages. This strategy is supported by differentiated capabilities known as "The Amcor Way," including Talent, Commercial Excellence, Operational Leadership, Innovation, and Cash and Capital Discipline. The Company operates two reporting segments under ASC 280: Flexibles and Rigid Packaging. As of June 30, 2020, the Flexibles Segment, which employs approximately 40,000 people across 181 manufacturing facilities in 39 countries, accounted for about 78% of consolidated net sales, while the Rigid Packaging Segment, employing approximately 6,000 people at 50 facilities in 11 countries, accounted for about 22% of consolidated net sales. Sales are primarily conducted through a direct sales force with offices and plants in Europe, North America, Latin America, Africa, and the Asia-Pacific region, and no single customer accounted for more than 10% of consolidated net sales in fiscal year 2020; sales to PepsiCo and its subsidiaries were approximately 11.1% and 11.0% in fiscal years 2019 and 2018, respectively, with arrangements aggregated across multiple contracts. The Company competes in highly competitive markets based on service, innovation, quality, and price, with key competitors including AptarGroup, Inc., Ball Corporation, Berry Global Group, Inc., CCL Industries Inc., Crown Holdings, Inc., Graphic Packaging Holding Company, Huhtamaki Oyj, International Paper Company, Mayr-Melnhof Karton AG, O-I Glass, Inc., Sealed Air Corporation, Silgan Holdings Inc., Sonoco Products Company, WestRock Company, and various privately held companies. The Company maintains inventory levels to balance favorable raw material pricing with timely order fulfillment and does not rely on any single supplier for major raw materials such as polymer resins and films, paper, inks, adhesives, aluminum, and chemicals, which are sourced globally. While raw material availability is currently stable, pricing may fluctuate. Amcor owns or licenses U.S. and international patents, trademarks, and trade secrets related to its products, processes, and equipment, which provide a competitive advantage, though the loss of any single patent or license would not have a material adverse effect on overall operations. The Company believes primary packaging remains essential for protecting and preserving food and healthcare products and is subject to environmental, health, and safety laws and regulations.

Chemicals serve as the major raw materials used by the company, sourced from a variety of global industry suppliers, with no significant dependence on any single supplier. While temporary industry-wide shortages of raw materials may occur, the company expects to continue managing raw material supplies effectively without significant supply interruptions. Currently, raw materials are readily available, though pricing may fluctuate. The company owns or licenses a number of United States and international patents and patent applications related to its products, manufacturing processes, and equipment, and holds trademarks and trademark registrations in the United States and other countries. Certain technology and processes are maintained as trade secrets. Collectively, these intellectual property rights provide a competitive advantage, but the loss of any single patent or license would not have a material adverse effect on overall results of operations or those of its reporting segments. Patents, patent applications, and license agreements will expire or terminate over time due to their terms or by operation of law. Amcor believes packaging plays a vital role in protecting and preserving food and healthcare products, extending shelf life, reducing product loss, and lowering carbon footprint and waste. Consumers prefer cost-effective, convenient, and easy-to-use packaging with end-of-life solutions to reduce waste. Amcor is committed to responsible packaging and, in January 2018, became the first global packaging company to pledge to develop all of its packaging to be recyclable or reusable by 2025, to significantly increase the use of recycled materials, and to collaborate with others to improve global recycling of packaging. The company is recognized for its innovation, holding thousands of active patents, and collaborates with customers, suppliers, and innovators to deliver industry-leading solutions and to enhance waste collection, sorting, and recycling infrastructure while informing consumers about the environmental impact of packaging. Amcor is uniquely positioned to lead in developing more sustainable and environmentally friendly packaging, which is seen as a key growth opportunity. The company’s operations and real property are subject to broad environmental laws and regulations across multiple jurisdictions, covering discharges of materials, waste handling and disposal, and cleanup of contaminated soil and groundwater. The company believes it is in substantial compliance with these regulations through its Environmental, Health, and Safety Management System and regular audits, though it cannot predict with certainty whether it may incur material liability for noncompliance due to contamination at former or current sites (including contamination from prior owners or operators) or off-site disposal of regulated materials. These laws and regulations are constantly evolving, and the company cannot always anticipate changes. For more details on legal proceedings, refer to Note 19, "Contingencies and Legal Proceedings," in the notes to the consolidated financial statements, and for a detailed description of relevant laws and regulations, see Item 1A. "Risk Factors." As of June 30, 2020, the company employed approximately 47,000 people worldwide, with about 42% covered by collective bargaining agreements. Relations with employees under these agreements remain satisfactory, and there have been no significant work stoppages or labor disputes in the past three years. The business of each reporting segment is not seasonal to any material extent. Research and development expenditures and policies are detailed in Note 2, "Significant Accounting Policies," of the notes to consolidated financial statements. Key risk factors include changes in consumer demand, where shifts in preferences for products or packaging formats may reduce demand for certain products or lead to obsolescence, despite mitigation strategies; key customer and customer consolidation risks, where loss of key customers or reduced production requirements could significantly impact sales and profitability, with sales to the largest customer accounting for approximately 11% of total net sales in fiscal years 2019 and 2018, and no single customer exceeding 10% of net sales in 2020 or any other period; competition in highly competitive geographies and end-use areas, where competitors may develop disruptive technologies or innovations that could harm competitiveness; challenges in expanding current business through organic growth or acquisitions, due to market saturation, changing customer plans, or difficulty identifying and acquiring suitable targets, especially given increased price multiples and competition for targets; integration challenges from acquisitions, including difficulties in merging business processes, systems, and cultures, and potential disruptions to operations, with the Bemis acquisition expected to generate approximately $180 million in pre-tax annual net cost synergies by the end of the third year from procurement, manufacturing, and general and administrative efficiencies, though full realization is not guaranteed; and intellectual property risks, where third parties could obtain information, independently develop similar technologies, or breach non-disclosure agreements, particularly in emerging markets where intellectual property protection is less robust, potentially reducing competitive advantages, causing lost sales, or requiring costly litigation or licensing; operational risks, including the impact of global health outbreaks such as the 2019 Novel Coronavirus (COVID-19), which has led to volatility in customer order patterns, temporary facility or supplier shutdowns, and a $25.6 million impairment of an equity method investment in the fourth quarter of fiscal year 2020 due to pandemic-related market declines.

To contain the virus, governments have implemented measures such as travel bans, gathering limitations, quarantines, shelter-in-place orders, and business shutdowns. These business shutdowns typically exclude essential services and critical infrastructure supporting them. The company has experienced minimal operational disruptions because it is largely considered to provide essential services. However, customer order patterns have been volatile in the second half of fiscal year 2020, and such volatility could persist in the future. In the fourth quarter, an equity method investment was impaired by $25.6 million, partly due to general market declines linked to the pandemic. See Note 7, "Equity Method Investments," in the notes to consolidated financial statements for further details. The outbreak has previously and could again lead to temporary closures of the company’s facilities, supplier, or vendor facilities. In limited cases, certain customers have temporarily shut down operations, affecting their demand, and the company may continue to face demand volatility from such shutdowns. The coronavirus has significantly impacted and may further impact the economies and financial markets of affected countries, negatively affecting economic growth, capital market functioning, foreign currency exchange rates, and interest rates. It may result in prolonged economic downturns, such as increased unemployment, reduced capital spending, business shutdowns, or recessions, which could reduce demand for customers’ products. Despite efforts to manage these impacts, the extent to which the coronavirus or other outbreaks affect the company’s operations—including its ability to secure financing at attractive rates—is unknown and could be material. Global economic challenges, including high unemployment in certain operating regions, low economic growth, and difficulties managing rising debt and economic volatility, have negatively impacted and may continue to negatively impact the company’s operations and financial results. Demand for the company’s products and services depends on consumer demand for packaged food, beverage, healthcare, personal care, agribusiness, industrial, and other consumer goods. General economic downturns in key geographic regions and globally can adversely affect the company’s operations and financial results. The current global economic challenges, including relatively high unemployment, low growth, and difficulties with rising debt and volatility in certain economies, are likely to continue exerting pressure on the global economy and the company’s business. The COVID-19 pandemic has increased global economic volatility. During challenging economic conditions, customers may delay, reduce, or cancel purchases, delay payments, or fail to pay, suppliers may struggle to fulfill orders, and distributors may face difficulties delivering products, all of which could impair the company’s ability to meet customer demands and result in lost business. Weakened global economic conditions may also lead to unfavorable changes in product pricing, product mix, and lower profit margins. All of these factors could adversely affect the company’s business, cash flow, financial condition, and results of operations, which effect may be material. Political uncertainty may also contribute to economic conditions in markets where the company operates. For example, the United Kingdom’s exit from the European Union has caused significant volatility in global financial markets and altered market behavior. Such political developments could disrupt markets served and tax jurisdictions, potentially leading to loss of customers, suppliers, and employees, and negatively impacting profitability. The company’s international operations expose it to various risks that could adversely affect its business and financial results. It operates globally, including in emerging markets. In fiscal year 2020, approximately 74% of sales revenue came from developed markets and 26% from emerging markets. The company expects to continue expanding, particularly in emerging markets. Managing global operations is complex due to substantial differences in cultural, political, and regulatory environments. Many countries where the company operates, including Argentina, Brazil, China, India, and other emerging markets, have underdeveloped or developing legal, regulatory, or political systems that are subject to dynamic change and civil unrest. The profitability of operations may be adversely impacted by: changes in fiscal or regulatory regimes; difficulties in interpreting or complying with local laws, including tax, labor, foreign investment, and foreign exchange control; nullification, modification, or renegotiation of, or difficulties in enforcing, contracts subject to local law; reversal of policies encouraging foreign investment or trade or relating to local agents or partners; pandemics such as COVID-19 affecting regions unequally; or changes in exchange rates and inflation, including hyperinflation, which may be worsened by the pandemic. Sustained legal, regulatory, or political instability in emerging markets could adversely affect the company’s business, cash flow, financial condition, and results of operations, which effect may be material. The international scope of operations includes limited sales to entities in countries subject to U.S. Office of Foreign Assets Control, U.S. Department of State, Australian Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade, and other national or supranational sanctions (collectively, “Sanctions”), and operations in countries periodically subject to Sanctions. This requires maintaining internal processes and controls. Failure to do so could result in employee breaches of laws and regulations, including those related to money laundering, corruption, export control, fraud, bribery, insider trading, antitrust, competition, and economic sanctions, due to lack of integrity or awareness. Any such breach could adversely affect financial condition and cause reputational damage, which effect may be material. Price fluctuations or shortages in raw materials, energy, and other inputs could adversely affect the business. As a packaging manufacturer, sales and profitability depend on the availability and cost of raw materials, labor, and other inputs, including energy. All raw materials are sourced from third parties, with primary inputs including polymer resins and films, inks and solvents, aluminum, and fiber-based carton board. Prices for these inputs are subject to substantial fluctuations due to changing economic conditions, pandemics (such as COVID-19), currency and commodity price fluctuations, resource availability, transportation costs, weather, natural disasters, political unrest, and other supply and demand factors. Increased costs can negatively affect business and financial results. Although the company uses strategies such as price adjustments with customers or increasing prices to offset input cost increases, there is no guarantee of anticipating or mitigating such movements, there may be delays in adjusting prices, and failure to do so could adversely affect business, cash flow, financial condition, and results of operations, which effect may be material. The company faces commercial risks, including operational disruptions such as mechanical or technology failures or forced closures due to pandemics (such as COVID-19), which could lead to production loss and increased costs; shortages in manufacturing inputs due to loss of key suppliers or their inability to supply; and risks related to development projects (such as cost overruns and delays). Many production and business locations are vulnerable to natural disasters, including earthquakes, snowstorms, hurricanes, forest fires, and flooding. Unplanned plant downtime at any facility would likely result in unabsorbed fixed costs that could negatively impact results of operations for the period. Supply shortages or disruptions in the supply chain—due to reliance on single suppliers or events such as the COVID-19 pandemic or natural disasters—could impair timely delivery of raw materials, equipment, and supplies, thereby affecting the ability to supply products to customers. Such disruptions could adversely affect business and financial results. In response to the pandemic, the company has implemented employee safety measures across all supply chain facilities, including proper hygiene, social distancing, and temporary screening, which are at a minimum compliant with local government regulations. These measures may not prevent the spread of COVID-19, and illness, travel restrictions, absenteeism, or other workforce disruptions could negatively impact supply chain, manufacturing, distribution, or other business activities. The insolvency or contractual default of any customer, supplier, or financial institution—such as banks or insurance providers—could significantly harm operations and financial condition. These risks are exacerbated during economic volatility (such as that caused by the pandemic), either globally or in specific geographies or industries. If a counterparty defaults on a payment, the company may be unable to collect the owed amount and may need to write it off. If a counterparty becomes insolvent or fails to meet obligations, the company may need to find a replacement or fulfill obligations itself, which would likely be more expensive. The occurrence of any such risk, including counterparty default, could adversely affect business, cash flow, financial condition, and results of operations, which effect may be material and result in a competitive disadvantage. A failure or disruption in information technology systems could disrupt operations, compromise customer, employee, vendor, and other data, and negatively affect business. The company relies on uninterrupted functioning of its information technology and control systems to manage operations and business functions, process, store, and report information, and interact with customers, vendors, and employees globally. Increasing reliance on cloud solutions requires different security measures, including technical network security improvements, organizational and governance changes, and alignment with third-party vendors on market standards. As with large systems, IT systems may be vulnerable to damage, disruption, information loss, or shutdown due to power outages, software or hardware failures, computer viruses, cyber-attacks, catastrophic events, telecommunications failures, user errors, unauthorized access, or malicious or accidental destruction or theft of information or functionality. The company maintains and accesses sensitive, confidential, or personal data subject to privacy and security laws and customer controls. Despite protective efforts, facilities and systems—including those of customers and third-party service providers—may be vulnerable to security breaches, misplaced or lost data, and user errors that could compromise such data. Information system damages, disruptions, shutdowns, or compromises could result in production downtimes, operational disruptions, transaction errors, loss of customers and business opportunities, violations of privacy laws, legal liability, regulatory fines or penalties, negative publicity, reputational damage, reimbursement or compensatory payments, and other costs, any of which could adversely affect business, cash flow, financial condition, and results of operations, which effect may be material and result in a competitive disadvantage. Although mitigation measures are in place, systems, networks, products, and services remain potentially vulnerable to advanced and persistent threats. The company’s continued success depends on its ability to identify, attract, motivate, train, and retain qualified personnel in key functions and geographic areas. Losing key employees could make it difficult to meet objectives. There is no assurance that the company will be able to recruit, train, assimilate, motivate, and retain future employees who meet cultural standards. The company is subject to costs and liabilities related to current and future environmental and health and safety laws and regulations that could adversely affect business. Compliance with environmental and health and safety laws, rules, and regulations in each country where it operates is required. Many products come into contact with food and beverages, so the company is also subject to local and international standards related to such products. Compliance requires significant financial and employee resources. Changes to such laws, regulations, and standards are regularly proposed, and some may directly or indirectly result in a material reduction in operating results. For example, increased legislation on plastic packaging litter or recycling may lead to bans or limitations on certain packaging formats or materials in some countries or regions. Increased regulation of emissions linked to climate change, including greenhouse gas (carbon) emissions, could increase operational costs due to compliance costs, higher fossil fuel inputs, and more expensive energy-intensive raw materials. However, the extent of such changes is uncertain, and the company cannot predict additional capital or operating expenses required for compliance. Federal, state, provincial, foreign, and local environmental requirements related to air, soil, and water quality, handling, discharge, storage, and disposal of substances, and climate change are significant factors in operations. Changes to such requirements generally increase operational costs. The company may face environmental liability for the costs of remediating contaminated soil or water at its owned, used, or operated facilities (including future acquisitions). Legal proceedings may result in fines, penalties, and mandated remediation programs requiring substantial, sometimes unplanned, capital expenditures. The effects of climate change and greenhouse gas emissions may adversely affect business. Numerous governmental bodies have introduced or are considering introducing regulatory changes to address climate change impacts, which, if implemented, could negatively affect operations or financial results. The company has incurred and may incur fines, penalties, legal costs related to environmental matters, and costs for damage to natural resources, lost property values, and toxic tort claims. Provisions are made when it is probable that liability exists. However, because the extent of potential environmental damage and the company’s liability is usually difficult to assess and may only be determined over a long period, actual liability may end up substantially higher than currently provisioned amounts. Additional charges could result, adversely affecting operating results and financial position, which may be material. The company is subject to the risk of labor disputes, which could adversely affect business. Although no significant labor disputes have occurred in recent years, there is no assurance that future disputes—including protests and strikes—will not arise, which could disrupt operations and negatively affect business and results of operations. Although relations with employees are currently good, there is no assurance that satisfactory working relationships will be maintained in the future. Financial risks include LIBOR-indexed borrowings and foreign exchange rate exposure. A substantial portion of the company’s borrowing capacity bears interest at a variable rate based on the London Interbank Offered Rate ("LIBOR"). In July 2017, the United Kingdom’s Financial Conduct Authority (“FCA”), which regulates LIBOR, announced its intention to phase out LIBOR by the end of 2021. The U.S. Federal Reserve, in coordination with the Alternative Reference Rates Committee—a steering committee of major U.S. financial institutions—is considering replacing LIBOR with the Secured Overnight Financing Rate ("SOFR"), a new index based on short-term repurchase agreements backed by Treasury securities. Some financing agreements include language to determine a replacement rate for LIBOR if needed. However, if LIBOR ceases to exist, the company may need to renegotiate financing agreements extending beyond 2021 that use LIBOR. The company is evaluating the potential impact of the transition from LIBOR, but cannot predict whether LIBOR will cease after 2021, whether SOFR will become widely accepted, or the impact of such a transition on business, financial condition, and results of operations. The company is exposed to foreign exchange rate risk, both transactional and translational. Transactional exposures arise from exchange rate fluctuations affecting costs (in currencies such as the U.S. dollar, Euro, or Latin American currencies) and sales proceeds. Translational exposures result from converting entity functional currencies to U.S. dollars for reporting purposes and may affect the reported value of assets and liabilities and income and expenses. In particular, translational exposure may be affected by movements in the exchange rate between the Euro and the Brazilian Real against the U.S. dollar. Exchange rates have varied in recent years and remain subject to further movement. Exchange rates between transactional currencies may change rapidly. For instance, the Mexican peso and the Brazilian Real have experienced such fluctuations.

In 2021, the company is evaluating whether the Secured Overnight Financing Rate (SOFR) will become a widely accepted benchmark replacing LIBOR, and assessing the potential impact of such a transition on its business, financial condition, and results of operations. The company is exposed to foreign exchange rate risk, both transactional and translational, which could negatively affect its financial performance. Transactional exposures arise from fluctuations in exchange rates involving the U.S. dollar, Euro, and other currencies, including those in Latin America, impacting input costs and product sales proceeds. Translational exposures occur when converting entity functional currencies to U.S. dollars for reporting purposes and may affect the reported value of assets, liabilities, income, and expenses, particularly due to movements in the exchange rate between the Euro and the Brazilian Real. Exchange rates between transactional currencies can change rapidly, as seen in the Mexican peso and Brazilian Real, which have faced significant devaluation due to economic concerns, including the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic. The company has recognized foreign exchange losses related to Argentina’s currency devaluation and its designation as a highly inflationary economy under U.S. GAAP, as detailed in Note 2 of the financial statements. Continued currency devaluation could lead to a lag in passing through U.S. dollar-denominated input costs, adversely affecting margins and profitability, and exposing the company to future exchange rate fluctuations that could materially harm reported cash flow, financial condition, and results of operations. Increases in interest rates could raise borrowing costs and negatively impact results of operations, particularly affecting interest payments on variable-rate borrowings, as noted in Note 13 of the financial statements. A downgrade in the company’s credit rating could reduce access to the commercial paper market, increase borrowing costs or fees, or widen credit spreads when issuing debt, due to assessments by credit rating agencies based on financial performance, industry outlook, and global economic conditions. The company has a hedging policy to manage interest rate and foreign exchange risks, but failure to hedge effectively, under-hedging, or a default by a hedge provider could adversely affect business, cash flow, financial condition, and results of operations. As of June 30, 2020, the company had $7.3 billion in goodwill and other intangible assets, which are reviewed annually or when impairment indicators arise using discounted cash flow methods. Future changes in cost of capital, cash flows, or business strategy—especially due to events like the COVID-19 pandemic—could result in impairment charges, which would reduce net operating results and net worth, with a significant write-down having a material adverse effect. The company identified two material weaknesses in internal controls during the transition from Australian Accounting Standards (AAS) to U.S. GAAP: a lack of accounting staff with U.S. GAAP experience and deficiencies in segregation of duties within key IT systems used for financial reporting. These were fully remediated by the end of fiscal year 2020, with ongoing efforts to implement new controls, automation, compensating controls, and training to address the second weakness, which will be considered remediated only after sufficient operational time and testing confirm effectiveness. Failure to remediate these weaknesses or identify new ones could impair financial reporting accuracy, damage investor confidence, and negatively affect the trading price of common stock. The company uses insurance policies, including through its captive insurance company, Amcor Insurances Pte Ltd in Singapore, to manage operational risks, but such policies may not fully cover all risks, and claims exceeding captive reserves could harm business, cash flow, financial condition, and results of operations. The company is subject to litigation and regulatory risks, including lawsuits and governmental proceedings arising from its global operations, with uncertain outcomes that could require substantial payments. Environmental, health, and safety regulations, especially those related to greenhouse gas emissions and climate change, could increase raw material, energy, and freight costs, restrict the use of certain materials, and require additional compliance costs, particularly in highly regulated markets like healthcare and food and beverage packaging. The company’s success depends on its ability to develop and introduce new products and maintain intellectual property rights through patents, trademarks, trade secrets, and licensing, but pending applications may not be approved, and competitors may challenge validity or scope, or develop non-infringing alternatives, potentially weakening its competitive position. The company is incorporated under the laws of Jersey, Channel Islands, which are based on English corporate law and differ from U.S. corporate law, and may not offer the same level of legal certainty or investor protection. U.S. shareholders may face difficulties enforcing civil liabilities against non-U.S. directors or officers, and judgments from U.S. courts may not be directly enforceable outside the U.S., including in Australia or Jersey. The company’s Articles of Association designate the Royal Court of Jersey as the sole and exclusive forum for certain shareholder and fiduciary actions, though U.S. courts may still have jurisdiction over claims under U.S. securities laws, and there is uncertainty regarding enforcement of the exclusive forum provision. The company’s principal manufacturing plants include 181 facilities in the Flexibles Segment across 39 countries, 130 of which are owned and 51 leased, with lease terms ranging from two to 36 years and renewal options; the Rigid Packaging Segment has 50 plants in 11 countries, 12 owned and 38 leased, with lease terms from two to 20 years and renewal options. The company’s principal executive offices are located in Zurich, Switzerland. The company’s ordinary shares are traded on the NYSE under the symbol AMCR and its CHESS Depositary Instruments are traded on the ASX under the symbol AMC. As of June 30, 2020, there were 100,310 registered holders of record. Amcor is a global leader in developing and producing responsible packaging for food, beverage, pharmaceutical, medical, home and personal-care, and other products, working with leading companies to protect products and people, differentiate brands, and improve supply chains through flexible and rigid packaging, specialty cartons, closures, and services. The company focuses on packaging that is increasingly lightweight, recyclable, reusable, and made with recycled content. In fiscal year 2020, approximately 47,000 employees generated $12.5 billion in sales from operations spanning approximately 231 locations in over 40 countries. The impact of the 2019 Novel Coronavirus ("COVID-19") introduced significant uncertainty; Amcor’s operations were recognized as essential by governments due to their role in supplying critical food and healthcare products. The company established three guiding principles: health and safety of employees, maintaining operations, and contributing to community relief efforts. Health and safety measures include global and regional response teams, restrictions on travel, quarantine protocols, and frequent disinfecting of facilities. Operations and supply chain plans were implemented globally to address infection prevention, incident response, return-to-work protocols, and supply chain risks. Despite minimal operational disruptions, customer order patterns were volatile in the second half of fiscal year 2020, particularly in April, when Rigid Packaging Segment sales in North America and Latin America declined due to reduced foot traffic in convenience and on-the-go channels. Facilities were largely exempt from government closure orders, and operations are expected to remain operational due to the essential nature of the products supplied. However, significant disruptions, including temporary closures, remain possible. The company has not experienced significant supply chain disruptions and continues to monitor risks. Amcor launched a global program to support communities by donating food and healthcare packaging and funding local initiatives to improve access to healthcare, education, or food. Looking ahead, the company believes it is well-positioned to meet the challenges of the pandemic but cannot reasonably estimate its duration or severity, which will depend on supply chain disruptions, social distancing measures, and macroeconomic recovery.
